open_obligations: Note that Engels et al.'s NSO model takes success as the product of the stepwise Guard win probabilities, so it does not measure error propagation between levels directly.
Check that the equal-slope assumption (mG = mH = 1) used for the numerical results is realistic.
Check whether 'oversight success' in Engels et al. corresponds to bounded reward-model error in Leike et al.
out.other_title: Do errors accumulate across levels of recursive reward modeling?
out.rationale: Leike et al. ask whether mistakes compound across levels of recursive reward modeling: whether the mistakes of the narrower agent A(k-1) lead to larger mistakes in training A(k), or can be dampened. Engels et al.'s NSO model plays a series of n games between Guards and Houdinis whose general Elos are spaced Delta_general/n apart, and picks n to maximise the product of the stepwise Guard win probabilities. With it they report that multiple steps of nested oversight can move Guard log odds from -3 to 3 in some regions, with the optimal number of steps growing with the general capability gap (Delta_general) at a fixed Delta_domain; in Houdini-favoured games (Delta_general < Delta_domain), one step of oversight appears optimal. Because each game is set by its Guard's and Houdini's general Elos and overall success is the product of stepwise win probabilities, the model does not show whether mistakes at one level lead to larger mistakes at the next, so neither record bears on the other's claim.
out.scope: proposed SHARES_TOPIC: oversight chained over several levels, in Engels et al.'s Elo-based model of nested scalable oversight and in Leike et al.'s hierarchy of agents trained with recursive reward modeling

out.other_title: Bootstrapping through intermediate model sizes improves weak-to-strong PGR on chess
out.rationale: Burns et al. report bootstrapping through two intermediate sizes improves PGR on chess, especially for larger students, but in preliminary experiments helps little on NLP and not on reward modeling. Engels et al.'s numerical NSO model finds multiple oversight steps can raise Guard log odds from -3 to 3, with more steps optimal as the general capability gap grows, but one step appears optimal in Houdini-favoured games; one is a training experiment, the other an Elo model of adversarial oversight games.
out.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: whether supervising a strong model through intermediate steps beats a single large weak-to-strong jump

text: The authors report that NSO is better than a single step of oversight: multiple oversight steps let Guards oversee much smarter Houdinis, in some regions moving Guard log odds from -3 to 3; that the optimal number of steps grows with Delta_general at fixed Delta_domain; that larger Delta_general at fixed Delta_domain makes oversight easier; and that in Houdini-favoured games (Delta_general < Delta_domain) one step appears optimal.
title: NSO findings: multi-step oversight beats one step as the capability gap grows
